paras: The Georgetown police clash was a street fight on the night of August 9, 1910, in the Georgetown section of Washington, D.C., between a policeman and a group of about fifteen Black men he had ordered to move on. Four of the men were sentenced in Police Court the next day to thirty to sixty days in jail. White papers outside the capital presented the fight as a "race battle" and a sign that authorities feared "real race riots" in Washington.

The Washington Herald said the arrests were meant to break up a gang living in "Foggy Bottom" about which Georgetown residents had complained. The Richmond Virginian placed the fight in a season of "almost constant race trouble" in Georgetown, citing the Johnson-Jeffries prize fight, the shooting of a Black man by two Fort Myer soldiers three weeks earlier, and an "indignation meeting" held by Black residents the previous Monday.

According to the Evening Star's report of the court hearing, the policeman, named as Johnston and as Johnson, ordered half a dozen men away from a moving picture theater at 28th and M streets and, when they grew profane, chased them and arrested two at the Georgetown end of the Pennsylvania avenue bridge over Rock Creek. As he started for the patrol box, the others tried to free the prisoners, wrenched away his nightstick and beat him, and he drew his revolver and fired in the air to drive them off.

The Richmond Virginian's dispatch gave a larger version, set at Pennsylvania avenue and Twenty-sixth street, in which the men rushed the patrolman, he swung his nightstick "with telling effect," and three white men joined a general fight fought with "whiskey bottles to revolvers." In that account three men were captured, the group made two more rushes until three more policemen arrived, and the rest fled to Foggy Bottom. The same dispatch said that as far as could be learned no one was shot.

In Police Court on August 10, Assistant United States Attorney Turner called the fight one of the worst instances of lawlessness his office had seen in a long time and asked for heavy penalties. Judge Aukam sentenced James Lomax to sixty days, Richard Wallace to forty-five days, and Henry Nolden and Albert Brown to thirty days each, on charges the Washington Herald gave as disorderly conduct. The Evening Star said more arrests might follow, but no later proceedings appear in the coverage.

The two Washington dailies treated the case as a police-court matter, with the Evening Star headlining "NEGRO RIOTERS SCORED" and describing "a gang of fifteen drunken Foggy Bottom negroes," and the Herald running a short "Four Negroes Sentenced" notice. Out-of-town papers raised the stakes: the Richmond Virginian put "NEGROES ATTACK ARMED OFFICERS" on its front page, described a "Howling Mob of Blacks," and quoted a police official warning that the capital could become "a scene of rioting."

A short wire item ran on August 10 and 11 under headlines such as "RACE RIOTS IN WASHINGTON" in New Haven, "RACE RIOT IN WASHINGTON" in Bemidji, and "Capital Fears Race War" in Fargo. Its longer versions, such as the Prescott Daily News's, quoted officials that unless radical action was taken "to curb the lawless negroes" the situation might get beyond control. All of these accounts came from the police and prosecution side, and none gave a version from the arrested men.

The wire said shots were exchanged, while the Evening Star mentioned only the policeman firing into the air and the Richmond Virginian reported that no one was shot. The wire also gave the charge as assaulting a policeman, while the Washington Herald, reporting the sentences locally, gave it as disorderly conduct.

reader.title: Georgetown police clash (1910)
bases: All accounts describe a policeman's attempt to move on and arrest Black men that became a fight in which he used his nightstick and fired his revolver, aided in one version by three white men, with four Black men jailed (A1, A2, A5).

The Evening Star and Washington Herald court reports, the Richmond Virginian dispatch and the wire item independently agree on a fight between a policeman and a group of Black men in Georgetown and the jailing of four of them (A1, A2, A3, A5).

accounts.gist: Another outbreak between Black and white people in Georgetown in which shots were exchanged and stones and whiskey bottles used; four Black men arraigned for assaulting a policeman, and authorities feared race riots.

framing.detail: The Evening Star headlined 'NEGRO RIOTERS SCORED' and called the men 'a gang of fifteen drunken Foggy Bottom negroes', relaying the prosecutor's call for heavy penalties.

The Richmond Virginian's front page ran 'NEGROES ATTACK ARMED OFFICERS' and 'Howling Mob of Blacks' and tied the fight to the Johnson-Jeffries fight, a soldier shooting and a Black 'indignation meeting'.
The wire ran as 'RACE RIOTS IN WASHINGTON', 'Capital Fears Race War' and with a subhead on 'Turbulent Blacks', quoting officers on curbing 'the lawless negroes'.
The Washington Herald gave a brief 'Four Negroes Sentenced' notice framing the arrests as breaking up a Foggy Bottom gang.
